thag7.1:1.4: The courtesan (_vesikā_) here is depicted as refined and cultured, deploying customary niceties and playful allusions as artfully as she does her carefully groomed appearance. Kauṭilya (Arthaśāstra 2.27) recommends that kings should sponsor the education of courtesans in “singing; playing musical instruments; reciting; dancing; acting; writing; painting; playing the lute, ﬂute, and drum; reading another’s mind (_paracittajñāna_); preparing perfumes and garlands; conversation; shampooing; and the arts of a courtesan” ( see note on [an3.39:2.2]()).
thag7.1:2.1: An indication of submission, in contrast with the haughty behavior of the brahmin lady of the Verahaccāni clan ([sn35.133:2.7]()).
thag7.1:2.2: In the Suttas, this gesture is only used in honor of esteemed spiritual masters.
thag7.1:3.1: She is familiar with the Vedic custom whereby a man goes forth only in the last stage of life. Rather than trying to make him abandon his spiritual quest, she urges that life with her would be fulfilling the proper stages of life.
thag7.1:3.2: She plays with the word _sāsana_, normally used for a religious “dispensation”.
